author: lpatiny
body:
Speeds up the hot loops of the distance and similarity functions.

## Algorithmic changes

- **`kumarJohnson`**: `prod ** 1.5` → `prod * Math.sqrt(prod)`. No engine specializes a 1.5 exponent, so this is the biggest win, on V8 and JavaScriptCore alike.
- **`minkowski`**: special-case `p = 1` and `p = 2`. V8 sends `x ** 1` through generic pow at ~9x the cost of a plain read; `p = 2` is worth ~1.5x when called monomorphically.
- **`similarity.pearson`**: drop the two arrays it allocated only to mean-centre before calling `cosine`, folding the work into two passes.

Measured with `beforeAfter.js`, before → after, per element (n = 10000, Float64Array, node 24):

| function | before | after | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `kumarJohnson` | 15.50 ns | 2.41 ns | 6.4x |
| `similarity.pearson` | 19.06 ns | 3.23 ns | 5.9x |
| `minkowski(p=1)` | 11.51 ns | 2.02 ns | 5.7x |

For the other functions defining const like for example from:

```js
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    ans +=
      a[i] * Math.log((2 * a[i]) / (a[i] + b[i])) +
      b[i] * Math.log((2 * b[i]) / (a[i] + b[i]));
  }
```

to

```js
 for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    const ai = a[i];
    const bi = b[i];
    const sum = ai + bi;
    ans += ai * Math.log((2 * ai) / sum) + bi * Math.log((2 * bi) / sum);
  }
```

has no impact, neither with bun or with nodeJS except in the case of polymorphism (once a typed array, once a number array for example) and in this case we win a factor 1.5

But as a side observation changing the type of an array is really a bad idea and we are loosing a factor 2 in speed. I wonder if we can reach this kind of issue in some of our projects.

So practically I would still make this 'const' definition even if we win speed only in case of polymorphism. @targos WDYT ?

author: cohemm
body:
Closes #1756.

First of three slices carved out of the closed combined PR #1749. This one is
independent of the other two: it is about file modes only, and touches neither
the advisory lane (#1754) nor interview provenance (#1755).

## Purpose

An interview transcript holds what the user typed, verbatim. A Seed holds what
was distilled from it. Auto pipeline state holds the same answers for as long
as the session record exists. All three are written at the umask default —
typically `0644` — and stay world-readable for their whole lifetime.

## What changed

`core/owner_only.py` is one primitive: create at `0600`, temp file plus
`os.replace`, fsync the parent directory, return whether durability was
confirmed. Five writers now call it.

| Writer | Was |
|---|---|
| `InterviewEngine.save_state` | `_atomic_write_text`, mode preserved |
| `_plugin_save_state` | `write_text`, no atomicity |
| `SeedGenerator.save_seed` / `save_seed_sync` | `write_text` |
| `PMInterviewEngine.save_pm_seed` | `_atomic_write_text` |
| `auto/adapters.py`, `auto/state.py` | `write_text` |

`interview.py`'s local `_atomic_write_text` is removed. It was careful about
atomicity and about *preserving* an existing mode, but a file it creates starts
at the umask default and preservation then keeps it there.
`cli/commands/setup.py` keeps its own same-named helper — those config files are
meant to be readable.

An existing `0644` file is narrowed on the next write rather than preserved.
Preserving it would mean the fix never reaches anyone already installed.

Directories are deliberately left alone. `seeds_dir` and Auto's `root` may be
caller-supplied and shared, and narrowing a directory this package does not own
is not its call. `state_dir`, which Ouroboros does own, is created secured.

## Success criteria

- Every writer above produces `0600`, including the plugin transport and both
  Auto paths.
- A file that already exists at `0644` is narrowed on the next write.
- A failed `os.replace` leaves the previous file intact with its content
  unchanged; an unconfirmed directory flush is logged and the caller's success
  return is unchanged.
- Caller-supplied directories keep their own permissions.
- `tests/unit`: 13,281 passed. Three failures are pre-existing and unrelated —
  two build a wheel via `uv build`, which cannot reach the network in this
  environment, and one asserts on orphaned-session cleanup; all three fail
  identically with this branch's changes stashed.

Two existing tests pinned the old contract and are updated rather than deleted:
mode preservation becomes mode narrowing, while the atomicity and fd-hygiene
assertions around them are kept and now cover the new writer.

author: asksrilaprabhupada
body:
The V2 branch returned *before* the caching logic, so every request recomputed the whole pipeline. `cache.ts` existed but nothing called it for full responses.

This matters more since the move to MICRO: `max_connections` is **60**, and each request opens **five** concurrent RPCs.

## Key discipline

Keyed on the **exact normalised question + mode + corpus version**. A semantically-close but *different* question never reuses the entry — answering one devotee's question with another's evidence is how words get put in Śrīla Prabhupāda's mouth by accident.

**A degraded or evidence-insufficient response is never cached.** It's correct but weaker, and a 24-hour entry would outlive the outage that produced it.

Cache reads and writes are both non-throwing: a cache that is down costs latency, never a search. The per-request fields (`searchLogId`, `requestId`) are stripped before storing — each serving logs its own row and carries its own correlation id.

## Tests

Covering the invariant that actually matters, the keyspace:

| Assertion |
|---|
| same question, same mode → stable across case / whitespace / trailing `?` |
| `"krsna loves the devotee"` ≠ `"the devotee loves krsna"` — word order carries meaning |
| `quick` and `guided` are separated |
| corpus version is in the key, so a re-tagged corpus cannot serve stale answers |
| the raw question never appears in a key |
| embeddings keyed by **model**; reranks keyed by question **and** candidate set |
| candidate-set hashing is order-independent |
| a throwing cache still yields the produced value |

## Gates

`lint` 0 errors · `typecheck` clean · **175 tests** · production build succeeds.

Also appends the finishing-pass addendum to `docs/PHASE_CD_REPORT.md` — what was fixed after the four phases merged, and what remains open with the reason.

author: hmbown
body:
No-Issue: partial slice of #3897 — this removes the quadratic parse; the render half stays open.

Refs #3897.

## What changed

`markdown_render::parse` re-parsed the entire growing message on every streamed chunk — quadratic over message length, which is why a long answer got slower the longer it ran.

The parser was *already* strictly line-oriented: every source line maps to blocks using only a three-field carry (`in_code_block`, `code_language`, `code_block_id`). That property is what makes resuming **exact** rather than approximate — appending text can never change how an earlier complete line parsed. So `parse` is now built on a resumable `ParseState` that commits whole lines and re-parses only the trailing partial line, memoized per render thread.

Two deliberate safety properties:

- **Resumption is verified, not assumed.** The committed source prefix is kept verbatim and compared byte-for-byte before reuse. A different cell, a shrunk buffer, or an edit to earlier bytes fails the check and falls back to a full parse. A miss costs exactly what the old code always paid, so this can only be faster or identical — never wrong.
- **The trailing partial line is never committed.** Streaming can still extend it, and committing it early is the one way this could diverge.

The line-classification body was extracted verbatim into `push_parsed_line`, called by both paths, so batch and streaming cannot drift.

## Honest scope: this is the parse half only

The issue's acceptance says *"streaming a large message shows flat (not growing) per-chunk render cost."* This PR removes the quadratic **parse**; `render_parsed` still re-renders every block per chunk, including syntax highlighting, so per-chunk cost is now linear rather than flat. Splitting the render half safely means reusing rendered lines for a stable block prefix, and block grouping (tables, lists) makes a naive prefix split risky on the render hot path.

I am leaving **#3897 open** and referencing rather than closing it. The remaining work is the render-side cache, plus the live-TUI verification the issue asks for, which I cannot perform.

## Receipts (macOS)

- `incremental_parse_matches_a_full_reparse_at_every_prefix` — a corpus covering fences opened/closed across chunk boundaries, an unterminated fence, tables, nested lists, rules, blanks, CRLF and CJK is parsed at **every byte prefix** and compared against a cold full re-parse. Compares the whole AST, so any field of any block diverging fails.
- `streaming_does_not_reclassify_committed_lines` — 400 streamed chunks classify **400** lines, not the 80,200 a quadratic parse would.
- `a_changed_prefix_is_not_resumable` and `interleaved_sources_do_not_contaminate_each_other` — the fallback and multi-cell cases.
- `codewhale-tui` 8345 passed / 0 failed; `qa_pty` 25 passed / 0 failed; CI's exact clippy invocation, fmt, and diff checks clean.

author: samovers
body:
Part of #192. Follows merged #233.

## Primary trust boundary

Production runtime construction and startup admission of the pre-tenant audit database graph.

This PR changes only the startup connection topology and its focused verification. Not provisional.

## Problem

The five configured pre-tenant audit startup routes opened PostgreSQL connections without code-owned connection or statement bounds. The audit-control authority probe then closed its connection and the HMAC lifecycle observation opened a sixth connection, so that first observation was not covered by the authority probe's connection identity.

## What changed

- Keep exactly five configured startup database routes: tenant readiness, audit readiness, authentication producer, request-router producer, and audit control.
- Open every authority-probe connection with `connect_timeout=5` and PostgreSQL startup options `-c statement_timeout=2000`.
- Install both limits in `psycopg.connect()` before the first SQL statement; no later `SET statement_timeout` mechanism exists.
- Override conflicting timeout values embedded in a DSN with the code-owned arguments.
- Reuse the exact still-open audit-control connection for both its `SESSION_USER` probe and the correlation-HMAC database observation.
- Remove the separate sixth control-observation connection.
- Leave request-time audit-client factories unchanged.
- Execute the real Psycopg conninfo merge and real HMAC observer borrowed-connection path in tests.
- Use separate, explicit startup and request-time connection factories.
- Keep the composed startup-order test limited to events it actually observes; the real five-connection test proves lifecycle observation.

## Accepted invariants

- `AUDITTIME-001`: the runtime topology contains exactly the five named configured startup routes.
- `AUDITTIME-002`: each route receives the fixed five-second connect timeout and startup-installed two-second statement timeout before SQL.
- `AUDITTIME-003`: DSN values cannot weaken either timeout.
- `AUDITTIME-004`: every route performs its exact code-owned `SESSION_USER` probe.
- `AUDITTIME-005`: the audit-control probe and HMAC database observation use the same connection object.
- `AUDITTIME-006`: no sixth connection is opened for the control observation.
- `AUDITTIME-007`: timeout, authority, or observation failure remains fail-closed, closes the connection, and preserves the original cause.
- `AUDITTIME-008`: request-time audit delivery behavior and environment configuration remain unchanged.

## Operational facts

The five-second libpq connect timeout applies per host attempt. Code-owned PostgreSQL startup options replace any `options` embedded in a DSN. The audit-control connection remains open, idle, and outside a transaction during the bounded KMS posture calls. These consequences are stated in `kernel/README.md`.

## Non-goals

No database migration, role, grant, SQL API, audit producer/client, retry, health, overflow, gap, retention, export, KMS lifecycle, IAM, scheduler, multi-host policy, observer interface, or general database-timeout change.

## Anti-bloat budget

- `kernel/security_audit_runtime.py`: 189 / 200 lines.
- Focused runtime test module: 489 / 500 lines.
- The runtime cap was raised from 180 after exact-head review showed the former limit was selecting compressed syntax and removing useful names. The new cap remains firm while leaving design and readability in charge.
- No new production module, environment setting, `Any`, compatibility path, retry, background worker, or state machine.
- No function exceeds 80 lines.

## Verification

Exact head: `0576937`.

- Runtime topology/refusal plus real HMAC observer tests: 76 passed.
- Affected runtime, application-runtime, HMAC-posture, and architecture tests: 111 passed.
- Ruff on changed Python files: passed.
- Rewrite architecture budgets: passed.
- Package contract: passed immediately before every commit.
- Deterministic inventory remains 1,882 pinned tests; no test identity changed in this correction.
- `git diff --check`: passed.

The repository's inherited macOS Unix-socket path exceeds the platform's 103-byte limit from this long worktree. The complete deterministic PostgreSQL baseline remains the pinned Linux CI responsibility.

## Review disposition

Both earlier exact-head reviews found no Blockers. The second review correctly observed that the 180-line cap had begun choosing syntax over clarity. This correction raises only the local runtime guardrail, restores explicit connection paths and named observations, and removes the self-fulfilling lifecycle-order event. Widening the HMAC observer factory annotation and changing multi-host or arbitrary DSN-option policy remain cross-boundary Follow-ups.

Review against exact head `0576937`. A Blocker must identify a violated accepted invariant or provide a reproducible in-scope failure. Cross-boundary work is a Follow-up; optional alternatives are Preferences.

author: jwilleke
body:
Closes #951.

Two defects, one root cause — the seeder’s page-level failures were too quiet.

## 1. Duplicate uuid was undetected

Two source pages sharing a uuid — the obvious copy-paste mistake when creating a page from an existing one — meant the second file matched the first’s already-seeded page and was silently skipped. **One page simply never appeared**, and the only trace was a `debug` line phrased as normal operation. With reseed enabled it is worse: the two files fight over one page and the winner depends on filesystem ordering.

Now caught before seeding, naming both files and the shared uuid.

## 2. Missing/invalid uuid was type-blind

A domain addon’s page failing to seed is a broken site; the same failure in an additive addon is a missing help page. `AddonsManager.ts:~535` already draws exactly that distinction for identity mismatch — `error` for domain, `warn` otherwise. Page seeding now follows it.

## Both now outlive the boot

Each failure raises an operator notification. A boot-time log line is invisible ten minutes later, which is how a page that never seeded stays missing for weeks.

## Still not fail-fast

Per the explicit rejection recorded in #951: refusing to start because a third-party addon shipped one malformed page turns an authoring typo into an outage. The #672 precedent does not transfer — that was the operator’s *own* config naming a nonexistent addon, which the operator can fix. A vendor’s malformed file is not in the operator’s control.

Skip the page, report loudly, surface it after boot. There is a test asserting seeding resolves normally on a malformed page.

## Verification

6 new tests, including the two that matter most: a bad file does not abort the rest of the seed, and domain vs additive really do log at different levels.

Suite 6778 passed, tsc and lint clean.

author: gdevenyi
body:
Fixes #182.

`test_affine_agrees_with_the_paravision_nifti_sform` tripped its own `assert sform_code > 0` before it ever compared a matrix, and skipped entirely in CI — so it reported nothing either way.

### Read the form the writer populates

NIfTI-1 stores the affine two independent ways and a file need only carry one. All 14 `PV360_StdData` exports write the quaternion (`qform_code=1`) and leave the sform zeroed — method 2, squarely within the standard — while the helper read offset 280 regardless.

Decoding the qform instead, **the export agrees with the VisuCore-derived affine to 4.8e-07 everywhere**: obliques, the negative-determinant `UTE3D` volume and the diffusion series included. The oracle was sound the whole time and silently confirming the geometry.

`nifti_affine` now takes the sform when there is one, the qform otherwise, and fails only if a file declares neither — so it keeps working if a future ParaVision writes both.

### Cover what is on disk

Coverage follows the `nifti/` directories that exist rather than a hardcoded five, which brings in the four diffusion reconstructions plus `T2map_MSME`, `T2star_FID_EPI` and `T2star_map_MGE`: **14 reconstructions, 166 volumes**. Every volume of an export is checked instead of whichever one `glob` happened to yield first, which also pins each export as internally consistent (they are — spread 0.0 within every directory).

Where no corpus is present the parameter set is empty and the test skips cleanly, rather than erroring on `next()` of an empty glob as it did before.

### Make it run in CI

`conftest` smudged only `2dseq`, `traj` and `rawdata.job*`, so the `.nii` files stayed LFS pointers and `nifti_affine` took its skip branch. `.nii` is now required media — 54 MB of a 1.7 GB dataset.

The cache key gains a `-nifti` suffix, because `actions/cache` does not re-save on a hit: without the bump the newly required files would be re-downloaded on every run instead of once. **Drop that hunk if you would rather pay the download than invalidate the cache** — the rest of the change works either way.

### Verification

- 14/14 pass locally, over 166 `.nii` files.
- Negative control: the assertion rejects a missing RAS flip, a 0.1 mm origin shift, and a slice-direction sign flip. It is discriminating, not vacuous.

author: joejoeflyn
body:
LoadPreset memoises every parsed preset in an in-process cache that is only
invalidated by SaveStorePreset in the same process. That assumption holds for
the embedded bundle, which is immutable for the binary's lifetime, but store
presets are not: lerd install, lerd service update and the 24h refresh all
rewrite the store cache files from their own CLI process, and a running lerd-ui
never notices, serving the stale parse until the next restart.

The cache entry now records the store cache file's mtime, and LoadPreset
re-parses when it changes. The embedded bundle has no on-disk file, so its
entries keep the parse-once behaviour. This is the same shape as the framework
store's mtime-keyed cache.

Closes #1182

author: xroche
body:
Four conventions, each one something a recent PR got wrong first and fixed second.

Two are security rules. The `*_safe_` helpers abort on overflow, which is right for our own data and wrong for a cache or a header, where it trades a memory smash for a crash on malformed input; #717 and #732 both reached for `strlcpybuff` before that distinction was written down. And a compiler warning class is not the unsafe set: `-Wformat-truncation` only sees a *bounded* `snprintf` whose return is dropped, so #715 was scoped off a warning list that structurally could not contain the nine unbounded `sprintf` calls #722 then had to find by hand.

Two are test-design rules. A canary compared against `'\0'` cannot see the stray NUL an off-by-one terminator writes, which is the one bug it exists to catch, and neither ASan nor `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` sees an overflow landing inside the same struct. A bounds test that oversizes one field cannot distinguish a per-field bound from a single hardcoded one, nor from a fix that bounds that field and leaves its neighbours raw; both #717 and #732 shipped a test with exactly that hole and had it found in review.

Docs only.

author: laurentcoll1
skyphusion-rollins
body:
## What this fixes

Closes the mechanism behind #148. The full root-cause writeup is
[on the issue](https://github.com/skyphusion-labs/vivijure-control-plane/issues/148#issuecomment-5085007762);
the short version:

**The driver did NOT run out of invocation budget.** `provision_jobs.lease_until` was written only by
`setJobRunning` and by each step `mark()`, so it meant "a step boundary happened within the last 60
seconds", never "a driver is alive". `runpod_endpoints` is the one step that breaks that: a single
uninterrupted call that creates four endpoints and marks nothing inside itself. On a slow RunPod
account (~87s in that step during the cp#117 rehearsal) the lease lapsed at ~68s under a healthy
driver, the next poll won the now-free claim, and `continueProvisionJob` refused (it will not resume
anything short of `wfp_upload`) by writing `finishJob(failed)` + `setTenantStatus(failed)` + a
destructive rollback.

That reproduces BOTH reported facts with no invocation dying: the terminal message is the keyless
refusal verbatim, and the terminal step is `runpod_endpoints` because `inferStep` maps four completed
steps to it.

## The change

- **`renewJobLease`**, and a driver that beats it every 20s for as long as its invocation lives. An
  expired lease now means a dead driver and nothing else, so the `wfp_upload` boundary is reachable
  at ANY prefix duration instead of only a fast one (issue point 2).
- The heartbeat renews `lease_until` and **not** `updated_at`. Liveness and progress are different
  facts; bumping both would make a live-but-wedged driver immortal against the 10-minute lost-driver
  rule.
- **`updateJobProgress` and `renewJobLease` refuse a TERMINAL job.** A driver that lost its job runs
  on to the end of its invocation, and its late mark used to overwrite the terminal step and re-arm
  the lease on a failed row.
- `JOB_LEASE_SECONDS` moves to `store.ts` beside `leaseIsLive`, and `index.ts` reads it instead of
  keeping its own `60` that agreed by luck.
- `setInterval`, not `deps.sleep`, and the coupling is the point: `deps.sleep` models a bounded wait
  the flow AWAITS, while this is a background tick whose lifetime IS the invocation. When the
  invocation dies the timer dies with it.

### Repaired for free, same column

`claimReclaim`, `beginTeardown` and `jobHasLiveDriver` all refuse to act while a provision driver
holds a live lease. During a slow `runpod_endpoints` they read "no live driver", so a reclaim could
have blanked the tenant resource columns underneath the running provisioner. Not touched, fixed.

### Deliberately NOT changed

- **The cp#124 first-poll constant.** A later poll changes discovery time, not outcome, and an
  EARLIER one would have made the old race more likely, not less.
- **The yield boundaries.** `runpod_endpoints` still suppresses the yield and carries through to
  `wfp_upload` in one invocation.
- `tenant-studio-upgrade.ts` has its own driver and is not heartbeated here: no poll-driven
  continuation claims that job kind. Worth a follow-up, out of scope for this issue.

## Evidence

- `npm run typecheck`: clean.
- `npm test`: **825 passed, 34 skipped** (was 816 before; +9 new).
- **The discriminator was watched failing.** With the heartbeat stubbed out, "a poll CANNOT claim the
  job while the driver is still inside a long runpod_endpoints step" fails with
  `expected false to be true` on `jobHasLiveDriver`, which is the production symptom exactly.
- **Positive control inside the same test:** a second job takes the same 60s lease at the same
  instant with no driver behind it, and after the same 90s advance it IS claimable. So the `false` on
  the driven job is the heartbeat and not a harness that never expires anything.
- **The store guards are proven against real SQLite** (`store-d1-sql.test.ts`, the un-stubbable
  seam), and all three fail under mutation: bumping `updated_at` in the heartbeat, and dropping the
  status predicate from either statement.

## One thing I could not verify

Both readings of the fixture (driver alive past 109s, or driver dead before it) produce error_step
`runpod_endpoints`. The discriminator is whether `steps_done` on that job row actually contains
`runpod_endpoints`, plus its `provision.step` log line. I hold no `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN`, so I can
read neither prod D1 nor Workers Logs. Flagged rather than worked around; it is corroboration, and
the fix does not change shape either way.

Refs #148, #112, #124, #137.

body:
Closes #705

## Summary

Implements `defender/runtime/session_store.py` (the append-only per-case SQLite
session store) and `defender/runtime/selection.py` (render/ingest/fold on top
of it) per the committed spec (`defender/tests/spec_graph_705.yaml`), and
wires both through the runtime:

- **`driver.py`**: `build_agent`/`run_investigation` open the store, mint a
  `case_id`, write the run-dir pointer file, and attach the store-backed
  `ProcessHistory` capability unconditionally (the fold is the only thing
  `DEFENDER_COMPACTION` gates). `run_investigation` got a real `finally`
  (`_drive_agent`/`_flush_run_end`) that flushes the terminal exchange into the
  store on every exit — `UsageLimitExceeded`, `RunAborted`, `BudgetKill`,
  `StoreAppendError` — each with its own `truncated_by` value, plus a
  request-limit-aware guard in the store-render processor so a round that the
  framework is about to abort (it appends its own continuation to
  `ctx.state.message_history` *before* checking the limit) is never
  over-committed to the store ahead of the flush.
- **`observe.py`**: `write_trace` now projects `tool_trace.jsonl` from the
  store's `analysis`/`actor` reads instead of `logger.messages`. The wire log
  itself picked up two real fixes along the way: `RequestLogger.log`'s outer
  record `kind` was tagging itself off the *individual* dumped message's own
  `"kind"` field, so an embedded prior response mis-tagged as a second
  top-level response record and broke turn counting; and a second
  `RequestLogger` construction under one path now appends (preserving the
  first construction's lines) once the first has closed, rather than either
  always truncating or always raising.
- **The visualizer**: both `transcript.html` and `runtime.html` now open the
  store directly (`visualize_run._main_session_analysis`) and gained a new
  "Model transcript" section reading real `hydrate(role="analysis")` content —
  rendered through a new `esc_untrusted()` (in `visualize_primitives.py`) that
  HTML-escapes and additionally breaks `on<word>=`-shaped event-handler
  patterns with a zero-width space, since model-authored payload text is
  attacker-influenced by construction. `run_common.visualize()` now raises a
  new `VisualizeFailed` on a non-zero visualizer exit instead of swallowing it
  to stderr, so a run dir whose store cannot be resolved fails closed rather
  than silently rendering nothing (`run.py`'s own top-level call catches it to
  keep the CLI's overall exit code unaffected).
- **`scripts/testing/compaction_dryrun.py`**: unchanged — R13 kept it on
  `llm_requests.jsonl`, and it already handles the wire log's undelta'd
  verbatim dump correctly (confirmed by `test_compaction_dryrun_reader_survives_the_undelta_d_log`).

Two pre-existing test files were rewritten, spec-authorized by the spec's own
`test_the_pre_change_construction_assertions_are_overturned`: `test_compaction_driver.py`
(the old `investigation.md`-scanning fold/frontier glue driver.py deleted) and
`test_harness_b_construction.py` (the two-configuration `_main_extra_capabilities`
assertion, now unconditional).

Three *unrelated* pre-existing tests needed narrow updates once the store
existed for real, none of them weakenings:

- `test_budget_e2e_631.py::test_only_the_budget_kill_marks_truncated_by_budget` —
  asserted `truncated_by is None` on a request-limit exit under R27's old
  `{"budget", None}` domain; #705 (R4/R11) widens the domain to name every
  caught exit distinctly, so this now asserts `truncated_by == "request-limit"`.
  The property the test actually protects — a non-budget exit is never
  mislabelled `"budget"` — is unchanged.
- `test_salt_origin_647.py::test_replayed_message_zero_listing_matches_the_production_run_dir_file_set` —
  the allow-list of files legitimately written between `materialize_run_dir`'s
  snapshot and message 0 gained `session_store_pointer.json`, alongside the
  two wire-log files already there.
- `defender/runtime/observe.py`'s `RequestLogger` path-tracking fix above also
  fixed two *regressions* my own change introduced against
  `tests/e2e/test_query_tool_611.py` (two sequential same-path constructions)
  and `tests/test_curator_glm_survival.py::test_trace_per_spawn_distinct`
  (opening a `RequestLogger` on a path some *other* writer left content in
  must still truncate) — both now pass again.

## Adversary's verdict

An Opus adversary ran against the committed spec before implementation began
(detached worktree, no sight of this code). It surfaced 12 findings (H1–H12).
Two were load-bearing design choices I verified by hand-tracing the literal
committed tests before deciding to keep them as-is rather than "fix":

- **H1** — `ends_on_complete_pair` is `truncated_by IS NULL`, a status-flag
  check with no structural verification that the session's actual last row is
  a complete pair. Kept: no committed test distinguishes a mislabelled
  `truncated_by` from a structurally-verified read, and the flag is written by
  the same code path that determines completeness.
- **H12** — the render→ingest stamp handoff (`run_step`/`duration_ms`/`wire_sha`)
  is parked in a process-local `store.pending_stamps` dict rather than being a
  property of the row at the moment `render()` returns. Kept, after tracing
  `test_request_row_carries_run_step_duration_ms_and_wire_sha` by hand: an
  eager-insert alternative leaves an extra unstamped row in that test's exact
  sequence and fails it.

Three findings described designs I had already independently avoided while
writing the store (confirmed against the adversary's own descriptions, not
newly discovered from them): an in-process cache for frontier/fold identity
(mine is a store query keyed on `(session_id, boundary)`), an UPDATE-based
fold (mine mints-or-reuses via `SELECT` against a `seq`-keyed row, never
`UPDATE`s), and a depth-capped cycle guard on the parent-chain walk (mine uses
a proper visited-set, unbounded). The remaining findings from the same run
were incorporated during implementation; I don't have the adversary's original
report text to hand for a line-by-line accounting here (lost to context
compaction mid-session) — flagging that gap rather than reconstructing findings
from memory.

## Two known test failures — likely spec/fixture defect, not fixed

`DEFENDER_BUDGET_ENFORCE=1 uv run pytest tests/ learning/ -m "not live"` is
green except for the pre-existing 4 failures in `test_budget_enforcement_631.py`
(confirmed identical on `git stash` — unrelated to this branch) and two #705
tests:

- `test_store_driver_705.py::test_the_request_logging_guard_stays_around_the_log_path_only`
- `test_store_driver_705.py::test_run_end_flush_captures_the_terminal_response_on_every_exit`
  (its 4th, "uncaught exception" sub-case only — the other three pass)

Both fail for the same reason: their fake models return a **plain
text-only `ModelResponse` with no tool call** on the first call, and their
premise requires the MAIN agent to make a *second* model call afterward (an
encoding failure recovering and continuing, or a `RuntimeError` on the
in-fixture second call). Empirically, in this codebase's actual MAIN agent
construction (`build_agent_core`, no `output_type=`/output validator
anywhere), a text-only response with no tool call **always ends the agent

characteristic unrelated to the store; nothing in this PR's code path can make

## The bug
After 0.2.13 the recording pill stuck on its last state (usually "Transcribing...") while dictation itself kept working perfectly.

## Cause
The embedded tray icons shipped in 0.2.13 were shared long-lived instances, but H.NotifyIcon disposes the icon it replaces. The second time a state came round, its handle was already destroyed, so the assignment threw ObjectDisposedException inside the tray update. That exception escaped OnStateChanged before the overlay was told anything, so the pill never advanced.

The log showed it plainly: "A StateChanged handler threw" on every transition after the first.

## Fix
- hand out a fresh icon per assignment and release the one it replaced, so a disposed instance is never reused
- isolate the tray update, because one failing view of the dictation state must never stop the others

## Validation
- reproduced the exact failure against the old design and confirmed the new one holds across repeated state cycles
- dotnet build Scribe.slnx -c Debug (0 warnings)
- dotnet test (434 passed)

Also corrects the Store signing guidance: free Microsoft signing is MSIX only, so an MSI would buy a signing bill rather than avoid one. Releases as 0.2.14.

body:
## Summary

`/cepa:review` read exactly one roster (`## Review Agents (Active)`) and dispatched every agent in it on every run. There was no way to say *"this agent's findings are debt, not defects — run it weekly, not per-PR."*

Measured across 15 configured repos: the two most expensive (`dpc-pro`, `contexthub`) carry 13-agent rosters → ~17 agents per review round. Under `autonomy: full` and lfg's 3-round loop, a 5-worktree parallel session costs **~255 full-diff agent runs**. Three of those 13 are debt-accumulating, and one (`type-design-analyzer`) was already documented as *"use when new types/models are added"* — it was never meant to be unconditional.

## Changes

**`commands/review.md`**
- New `## Cadence` section; `argument-hint` gains `[cadence:weekly]`.
- `cadence:weekly` dispatches `## Review Agents (Weekly)` **instead of** Active — independent rosters, not base + overlay.
- Weekly scope = last 7 days of main-branch commits (`git log --first-parent --since` → oldest SHA → `git diff <sha>~1...main`). Empty window exits without a findings file.
- Skips the `learnings-researcher` and the entire conditional tier on weekly runs; records all three as `dispatched: false` / reason `cadence:weekly`.
- Weekly findings → `todos/review-weekly-*.md`, `scope: weekly:<date>`, **`status: deferred`**.

**`commands/setup.md`**
- Validates `## Review Agents (Weekly)`; flags agents in both rosters and an empty-but-present section.
- Codifies that a roster line with trailing prose (`- python-reviewer — not a Python project`) is a *corrupted agent name*, not an exclusion.

**Docs + manifests** — `README.md` (new "Review cadence" section), `CONFIGURATION.md` (reference + which agents must stay in Active), `plugins/cepa/README.md`; both manifests 1.10.2 → 1.11.0 in this commit.

## Why `status: deferred` at creation

This is what makes the loop close with no new machinery. [`/cepa:sweep` Step 2](plugins/cepa/commands/sweep.md) already drains `status: deferred` findings that are `mechanical`/`corroborated` with the originating branch merged — precisely the shape of debt findings over already-merged main commits. `pending` would strand them: a scheduled unattended run leaves nobody to triage, so they'd sit forever and the sweep would never see them. Semantically correct per `cepa:autonomy` §5 — a weekly run applies nothing by design, so every finding is a residual at creation.

Suggested usage, staggered ahead of the sweep (debt review Sunday, sweep Monday):

```bash
claude -p "/cepa:review cadence:weekly mode:headless"
```

## Fail-closed

body:
## Problem

Flashing a board whose bootloader vendor ID has no udev rule fails with a log that points nowhere useful:

```
[FIRMWARE_FLASHER] Selected port: usb_24012C822401
[USB DFU] Failed to open USB device: SecurityError: Failed to execute 'open' on 'USBDevice': Access denied.
[USB DFU] Script finished after: 0.01 seconds
[USB DFU] Could not release interface: 0 (TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'releaseInterface'))
[USB DFU] DFU Device closed
```

Two separate problems are visible here.

**1. The real cause is never stated.** With no udev rule for the vendor ID, the kernel leaves the device node root-owned:

```
$ lsusb
Bus 001 Device 085: ID 3997:df11 Xcorelabs DFU in FS Mode
$ ls -l /dev/bus/usb/001/085
crw-rw-r-- 1 root root 189, 84 /dev/bus/usb/001/085
```

WebUSB `open()` needs read **and** write access, so it gets `EACCES`, which Chrome surfaces as a `SecurityError`. The user sees only "Failed to open USB device" and reasonably concludes the app is broken.

`usbDeviceUdevNotice` ("Are **udev rules** installed correctly? See docs for instructions") already existed and is translated in some twenty locales — but `grep -rn usbDeviceUdevNotice src/` returns nothing. It was never wired up.

**2. Teardown logs a misleading TypeError.** `openDevice()`'s catch calls `cleanup()`, which calls `releaseInterface(0)` even though `open()` failed and `transport.usbDevice` is still `null`. The resulting `TypeError` is caught and logged, burying the actual error two lines up.

Surfaced by a new X-CORE Labs X32 board (`3997:df11`), but neither problem is X32-specific — any bootloader without a matching rule hits both. The missing X32 rule itself is betaflight/betaflight.com#739.

## Changes

- `usbdfu.js` — on a `SecurityError` from `open()` while `getOS() === "Linux"`, log `usbDeviceUdevNotice` alongside the existing failure message. Gated on Linux because udev is meaningless elsewhere, and on `SecurityError` because other open failures (device unplugged mid-flash) have nothing to do with permissions.
- `WebUsbDfuTransport.js` — `releaseInterface()` returns early when there is no device. Nothing was claimed, so there is nothing to release.

## Tests

New `test/js/usbdfu_open_failure.test.js`, 5 cases: the hint appears on a Linux access denial, is suppressed on Windows, is suppressed for a non-`SecurityError` failure, teardown still closes the device, and `releaseInterface` no-ops without a device.

Both behaviour tests were confirmed to fail with the two source changes stashed and pass with them applied, so they are not vacuous.

Full suite: 673 passed / 59 files. ESLint and Prettier clean.

## What changed

- add a hierarchical smooth Bernoulli history GLM with shared population trajectories and shrunken subject-specific deviation paths
- expose simulation truth, fitted population and subject trajectories, diagnostics, and an explicit population plug-in policy for unseen animals
- add a prospective factorial recovery benchmark spanning stationary identical animals, stable individual differences, shared drift, and individual drift
- document assumptions, boundaries, validation behavior, and a runnable example

## Why

Longitudinal behavioural models need to distinguish stable diversity from genuinely different learning trajectories. This is the first Unspool model that combines temporal drift with multi-animal partial pooling under the same model and validation contracts.

## Scientific validation

Across 20 replicates in each regime, the scientifically matched model wins under both mean realized subject-trajectory RMSE and held-out final-session log loss:

- stationary identical: complete pooling
- stable individual differences: static partial pooling
- shared drift: shared smooth model
- individual drift: hierarchical smooth model

All benchmark fits converge. The new model wins only in the regime it is intended to represent.

## Current boundaries

This slice uses fixed temporal knots, fixed regularization hyperparameters, a shared declared clock, dense joint MAP optimization, and local-Hessian uncertainty. It is a focused reference implementation rather than a general Bayesian inference engine.

author: zepedrorodrigues
body:
O Novo Banco: um só pedido, um só cabeçalho obrigatório (`x-nb-oc-channel`), e
a resposta mais rica dos dez. É o banco que prova o que a CGD não provava —
produtos ligados por omissão, erros estruturados como sinal, e finalidade que
muda o preço.

Tudo o que se segue foi medido a 2026-07-26 contra o simulador a sério. As
capturas estão em `internal/bancos/novobanco/capturas/`, uma por comportamento.

## O que a medição contrariou no dossiê

| o que o dossiê dizia | o que se mediu |
|---|---|
| o rendimento entra no preço | **não entra** — nem ele, nem profissão, vínculo, habilitações, situação profissional, NIF, tipologia ou localização. Variados um a um, deram todos o mesmo cêntimo |
| mista `{2..30}`, sem mais regras | o período tem de ser **estritamente menor do que o prazo** — 25 anos num prazo de 25 dá `V158`, a 26 passa. Nem a regra nem o código estavam registados |
| erros conhecidos: `V159`, `V126`, `V137` | há mais três: **`V157`** (na fixa, prazo ≠ período — e traz o prazo exigido lá dentro), **`V158`**, e **`V118`** (prestação acima de 7500 €) |
| prazo máximo = 75 − idade | é `min(escalão, 75 − idade)`, com o escalão a descer 40 → 37 → 35 aos 30 e aos 35 anos. **São os mesmos escalões do Montepio** |
| fixa a 30 anos → 5,24 % | a curva satura aos **20**: 20, 25 e 30 dão todos 5,270. Nove prazos, sete preços |

## Duas omissões que são afirmações

**Na mista a oferta sai sem fases.** O banco devolve uma TAN só — a do período
fixo — e não diz que taxa, que indexante nem que prestação se aplicam depois
dele. Publicá-la como se durasse o prazo todo era dizer que 3,992 % duram 30
anos quando duram 5. O `fases` não é exigido pelo contrato, e quem lê recebe
uma nota que o explica.

**`taxaIndexada` só sai como Euribor na variável.** Na mista é a taxa de
referência do período fixo, na fixa é a própria taxa base.

## O que isto traz ao KAN-35

A varredura de LTV ponto a ponto, a mesma que se fez à CGD:

| LTV | spread |
|---|---|
| 30 % a 50 % | 0,750 |
| 51 % a 70 % | 0,800 |
| 71 % a 80 % | 0,900 |
| 81 % a 100 % | 0,950 |

As quebras são em 50/51, 70/71 e 80/81 — **exactamente nas fronteiras do
`dominio.BandaLTV`**. A grelha de 5 % representa este banco sem perder um
cêntimo, e o preço **sobe** com o LTV. A CGD faz o contrário nas duas coisas:
desce, e quebra aos 67 %, que a banda de 5 % não representa.

⚠️ É o contra-exemplo que faltava. Um banco não decide a resolução da grelha;
dois mostram que ela tem de ser mais fina do que 5 % ou definida por banco. O
KAN-35 passa a ter as duas medições que precisava.

## Fidelidade

3002 ofertas confrontadas campo a campo com o corpo em bruto que as originou,
por um leitor independente — `map[string]any` e `float64` onde o nosso usa
struct com tags e `json.Number`.

**33 022 comparações, zero divergências.** Limite superior do erro de leitura:
**0,100 %** a 95 % de confiança (regra dos três). Custo para o banco: 4218
pedidos, 7,3 MB, 230 ms por simulação — um décimo do que a mesma amostra
custou à CGD, porque aqui não há página de 77 KB por cada fase fixa.

⚠️ Foi a preparação dessa corrida que apanhou a **cadeia de ajustes ao prazo**:
a idade encolhia-o pelo `V159` e a fixa encolhia-o outra vez para a lista dos
nove, e o segundo ajuste dizia «Pediu 35 anos» a quem tinha pedido 40. É o
mesmo defeito que a corrida da CGD apanhou lá. Passa a haver um só ajuste,
sempre contra o prazo que a pessoa pediu.

## Verificação: revertendo

| revert | resultado |
|---|---|
| na mista, declarar o `taxaIndexada` como Euribor | ✅ `TestMistaNaoInventaOQueOBancoNaoDiz` — «na mista o taxaIndexada é a taxa de referência do período fixo, não uma Euribor — veio 3.092» |
| na mista, publicar uma fase que cobre o prazo todo | ✅ `TestMistaNaoInventaOQueOBancoNaoDiz` — «o Novo Banco não publica o plano da mista; não se inventa um» |
| não reaplicar o prazo que o `V159` indica | ✅ `TestPrazoAcimaDoMaximoReaplicaOQueOBancoIndicou` — a simulação morre em `produto_indisponivel` em vez de repetir |
| deixar a cadeia de dois ajustes ao prazo voltar | ✅ `TestOsDoisEncolhimentosDoPrazoDaoUmSoAjuste` — «esperava um só ajuste, vieram 2: … de:35 para:30 nota:Pediu 35 anos» |
| na mista, deixar o período chegar ao prazo (tecto = prazo) | ✅ `TestMistaEncolheOPeriodoQueNaoCabeNoPrazo` |
| na fixa, não encaixar o prazo na lista dos nove | ✅ `TestFixaEncaixaOPrazoQueOBancoNaoPratica` — «esperava FIXA_10_ANOS com prazo 10, foi "FIXA_12_ANOS" com prazo 12» |
| mapear o arrendamento para habitação própria | ✅ `TestArrendamentoCustaMeioPontoDeSpread` + `TestOPayloadBateComOCapturado` |
| ignorar o indexante escolhido | ✅ `TestVariavelComEuriborEscolhida` — «pediu-se a Euribor a 3 meses e foi "INDEXADA_EURIBOR_12_MES"» |
| não anotar o desconto das bonificações | ✅ `TestBonificacoesVaoLigadasEODescontoFicaEscrito` |
| não enviar o `x-nb-oc-channel` | ✅ os 15 testes de captura |
| ler os montantes por `float64` | ✅ `TestVariavelLeOsNumerosDaCaptura` — «MTIC: esperava 356005.55, veio 356005.59» |

Portão inteiro: `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `go test -race ./...` verde.

## Fora de âmbito

- ⚠️ **O preço deste banco é um preço com desconto.** As duas bonificações vão
  sempre ligadas, porque são as de omissão do simulador e o `dominio.Pedido`
  não transporta selecção de produtos. A CGD simula sem os packs. A diferença
  sai como nota na oferta, mas a comparação só fica honesta com o **KAN-33**.
- O E2E do varrimento por este banco, à imagem do `e2e_cgd_test.go`, fica para
  um commit próprio — foi assim na CGD.

Closes KAN-10

author: giuliastro
body:
Both changes come from the same confusion: an app pointed at the wrong server looked like an app with broken models.

## The header names the harness

It showed only `host:port`. Which harness you are driving decides what the app can do — every per-backend limitation follows from it — and the same host can serve a different one, so the address alone is not enough to tell where you are.

The badge carries a distinct accent per harness and is sized to match the pills already in the app, rather than introducing a new scale. Mobile-first in the way that matters: the badge never shrinks and the **address truncates instead**, verified with a 60-character hostname at 375px — badge fully visible, no horizontal overflow.

Contrast measured for all six harness/theme combinations against their own composited background:

| | light | dark |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | 5.99:1 | 7.55:1 |
| Oh My Pi | 4.84:1 | 8.06:1 |
| PI | 4.84:1 | 9.42:1 |

The OpenCode badge uses `--primary-strong` rather than `--primary`, because `--primary` on `--primary-soft` measures 4.43:1 — under AA for 10px bold text. No new colour was invented for it; the token already existed.

## A failed model fetch says so

`Loading configured models…` rendered indefinitely when the fetch had actually failed, which reads as a slow server rather than a failure. This is what made a misconfigured server look like a broken feature: pointing the app at a server that does not know your session id returns `400 {"error":"Harness session not found"}`, and the UI said "loading" forever.

The error was already held in `modelLoadError` and shown in the model panel — just not where anyone looks. Every model label now goes through one value that names the failure, and the context chip marks it.

A model already known keeps showing if a later refresh fails: verified by stopping the bridge with a session open, where the chip correctly kept the model rather than blanking it. Losing good information to report a transient error would be worse.

Web 6/6 with new assertions covering both changes, build clean.

author: danilevyck-hash
body:
## Qué arregla

Las dos RPC de `/ventas` que quedaron afuera del arreglo del 25-jul (`ventas_topclientes_summary`, `ventas_clientes_detalle_summary`) filtran el año con:

```sql
WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM (fecha AT TIME ZONE 'America/Panama'))::int = p_anio
```

Función **sobre la columna** → no sargable → seq scan de `switch_facturas` entera (52.269 filas, ~58 MB de heap por el `raw_data` jsonb) en cada llamada, para cualquier año. Prueba dura: `ventas_topclientes_summary(2020)` devuelve `[]` y tarda **414 ms**.

`ventas_dashboard_summary` ya se había migrado (20260725170100) y está viva — verificado: `ventas_dashboard_summary(2020)` responde en 314 ms (≈ baseline de red), o sea corta en seco.

## Latencia medida (26-jul, contra producción)

| | régimen estable | 1ª llamada tras inactividad |
|---|---|---|
| topclientes 2026 | 271-417 ms (mediana 307) | **2.738-3.493 ms** |
| detalle 2026 | 491-749 ms | 993-1.514 ms |

Como la función barre la tabla entera, su costo depende por completo de si las páginas están calientes — y el caso que ve el usuario (abrir /ventas de a ratos) es justo el frío. Con rango + índice deja de depender de eso.

## Paridad — idéntica al centavo

Se reimplementaron las dos funciones **fuera de la base**, con aritmética decimal exacta (enteros escala 1e4, sin punto flotante), aplicando el filtro NUEVO, y se comparó contra la **RPC viva** en producción:

| año | topclientes | detalle |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 | 10 clientes ✅ | 163 clientes × 7 campos ✅ |
| 2025 | 10 clientes ✅ | 133 clientes × 7 campos ✅ |
| 2026 | 10 clientes ✅ | 121 clientes × 7 campos ✅ |

- Conjuntos de filas viejo vs nuevo: **idénticos** en 2022/2023/2024/2025/2026 (396 / 6.883 / 15.330 / 19.689 / 9.971).
- **Panamá = UTC-5 fijo** verificado fila por fila contra la tzdb en las 52.269 facturas: **0 discrepancias**.
- **Borde:** existe exactamente 1 factura cuyo año UTC no coincide con el año Panamá — `2025-01-01T00:06:53Z` = 31-dic-2024 19:06 en Panamá. Queda en 2024 con los dos filtros. Las 410 filas que caen 31-dic / 1-ene quedan todas en el mismo año.

## Por qué el detalle lleva solo cota inferior

Su CTE `sf` alimenta a tres consumidores y `last12m_filtered` **no tiene techo** (`fecha >= p_twelve_months_ago`), así que no existe rango cerrado válido. La cota es `LEAST(1-ene de p_anio-1, p_twelve_months_ago)` y se verificó que no descarta ninguna fila que las 3 CTE puedan usar.

## Cambio de cron (aparte)

`backup?grupo=switch` 19:15 → **23:30 UTC**. Es el único grupo que barre las tablas grandes (`switch_articulo_diario` 197k + `switch_facturas` 52k) y lo hacía a las 14:15 Panamá. Sigue dentro del **mismo día UTC** (el guard no-op de la 2ª oportunidad compara contra el día UTC). `EXTRA_ENTRY_HOURS_UTC` actualizado, y `cron-calendario.test.ts` ahora **deriva** esas horas de `vercel.json` en vez de repetirlas a mano.

⚠️ **Es higiene, no el arreglo de los picos.** Se probó la hipótesis de que ese scan enfriara la caché y disparara los picos: una observación lo sugirió, pero **3 ensayos controlados no la reprodujeron** (y en uno el pico apareció antes del scan). Queda documentado como tal.

## ⚠️ SQL a correr a mano (NO ejecutado)

`cxc/supabase/migrations/20260726190000_ventas_reportes_clientes_sargable.sql`

**CORRIDA 1 y CORRIDA 2 van en ejecuciones SEPARADAS del SQL Editor** — `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` no puede correr dentro de una transacción y el editor manda la pestaña entera como un bloque.

El índice nuevo (`idx_sf_fecha_cliente_cover`) hace falta porque `idx_sf_fecha_cover` **no lleva `cliente_nombre`**, que es justo la columna que estas dos funciones normalizan.

El código es tolerante a que no haya corrido: firmas y `RETURNS TABLE` idénticos, ningún archivo TS cambia.

- [x] `npx vitest run` — 1439 passed, 22 skipped (104 files)
- [x] `npx next build` verde

- [x] Paridad contra RPC viva en producción, 3 años, ambas funciones

author: wirkling
body:
Closes WORK-275.

**Stacked on [#3](https://github.com/wirkling/cumulus/pull/3) (WORK-274), which is itself stacked on [#2](https://github.com/wirkling/cumulus/pull/2) (WORK-273).** Base is set to the WORK-274 branch so this PR shows only WORK-275's diff. Merge #2 and #3 first.

## What this is, and what it deliberately is not

The plan for this ticket opens by admitting the node registry "already exists end-to-end", and it does. `nodes`, `node_capabilities` and `node_heartbeats` have been in `0001_init.sql` since the start; `packages/db/src/repos/nodes.ts` has `createNode`, `upsertCapabilities`, `recordHeartbeat`, `markStaleNodesOffline`; `/api/agent/register|heartbeat|capabilities` and the offline sweep are live. On top of that, the two siblings currently in flight have already claimed the parts the plan proposed adding:

| Plan item | Status |
|---|---|
| Persist node identity | **Shipped in WORK-273** — `machine_id` column, partial unique index, register dedup |
| Persist enrollment metadata | **Shipped in WORK-274** — enrollment tokens, approval, `/api/agent/enroll` |
| Registry tables + capability upsert + heartbeat status | **Already on `main`** |

Re-adding any of those would have produced a second, conflicting definition of something that now exists. So this PR adds none of them, and adds no migration.

What was genuinely missing is coverage. Three PRs are editing this exact surface concurrently and not one test holds its invariants still. `@cumulus/db` had **no test runner at all** — `pnpm --filter @cumulus/db test` failed outright, which is the first item on this ticket's own "Done when" list.

## Changes

**`@cumulus/db`** — gains `vitest` and a `test` script, plus:

- **`src/mappers.test.ts`** (pure, always runs) — row → domain for identity, capabilities and status. The lossy cases are the whole point: Postgres returns `numeric` as a *string* and `null` for an absent column, while the domain model says `number` and `undefined`. A regression here is silent — a node just quietly appears to have no identity, or no RAM.
- **`src/repos/nodes.test.ts`** (DB-gated) — the raw SQL that can actually break:
  - the `on conflict` capability upsert converges on re-report instead of accumulating rows;
  - `recordHeartbeat` stamps `last_heartbeat_at` and stores metrics, but **never** overwrites an operator's `draining`/`maintenance`/`disabled` decision — while still recording that the box is alive;
  - `markStaleNodesOffline` flips only stale `online` rows, leaves operator states and already-offline rows alone, and is idempotent;
  - registry rows reach `getPlacementCandidates` with capabilities intact and operator states marked `unavailable`.

**`@cumulus/api`**:

- **`src/routes/agent.heartbeat.test.ts`** (always runs, database mocked) — heartbeat and capability-report route contracts: auth (unknown node, revoked token, wrong token), validation (status outside the union, unknown capability fields against the `.strict()` schema), and what actually reaches the repo.
- **`src/routes/nodes.registry.db.test.ts`** (DB-gated) — the full loop over real rows, which is the only place the agent routes, the repo SQL and the operator projection are exercised together: register → `201` + `nodeId`; heartbeat → `{ ok: true }`; `GET /api/operator/nodes` showing capabilities and latest metrics; `GET /api/operator/nodes/:id` showing an advancing `lastHeartbeatAt`; and a drained node that keeps its operator status through an `online` heartbeat.

The DB-gated files follow the convention WORK-273 established: opt in via `CUMULUS_TEST_DATABASE_URL`, deliberately *not* `DATABASE_URL`, so a stray test run cannot write rows into whatever database happens to be configured.

## Deferred: `provisioning_state` — needs a human decision

The plan's one genuinely net-new item was an optional `provisioning_state` column carrying the `NEW → CONNECTING → … → ONLINE` bootstrap lifecycle. It is **not** in this PR, and the reason is a collision rather than a shortcut:

- That lifecycle already exists, defined exactly once, as **`BootstrapState` in `packages/shared-types/src/bootstrap.ts` on WORK-271** ([#1](https://github.com/wirkling/cumulus/pull/1)) — deliberately placed in shared-types with a comment naming this ticket as a consumer.
- WORK-271 is based on `main`; this branch is based on WORK-274. **`bootstrap.ts` does not exist on this base.** Adding a `ProvisioningState` union here would create a second definition of one concept, on a branch that cannot see the first — precisely the drift `bootstrap.ts` was written to prevent.
- The plan itself flags the underlying question as open: WORK-271 already persists this state machine **client-side** in the CLI's run-store (`BootstrapRunState`). Whether the control plane should *also* persist it is a boundary decision, not an implementation detail.

The corresponding "Done when" item is conditional (*"If provisioning-state is in scope…"*), so nothing is left unticked. **What a human needs to decide:** whether fleet-level provisioning state belongs in the control plane at all, and if so, this should land on a base that contains #1 so it can reuse `BootstrapState` rather than redefine it.

## Verification

Verified against a throwaway `postgres:16` container (removed afterwards):

- all 10 migrations — including the siblings' `0009` and `0010` — apply clean;
- `@cumulus/db`: **25/25 pass** (10 mapper + 15 repo);
- `@cumulus/api`: **46/46 pass** (33 always-on + 13 DB-gated).

Default run, no database configured — DB-gated suites skip as designed:

- `pnpm typecheck` — clean across all 7 projects;
- `pnpm test` — **91 passed, 28 skipped**.

The operator-state invariant was checked for substance, not just for green: inverting the guard in `recordHeartbeat` fails exactly the three tests that assert it, and nothing else.

`pnpm lint` was not used as a gate — it fails on `main` for an unrelated pre-existing reason (`apps/dashboard`'s deprecated `next lint` prompts interactively and exits 1 in a non-TTY).

No migration added. No change to `main`'s runtime behaviour — this PR is tests plus one `package.json` script.

body:
`medical_records.panel` is the document's own section heading, and the issue's premise checks out against the code and the seeded corpus: in practice it is **provenance**, not clinical meaning. The top stored values are `Quest Diagnostics` (89), `LabCorp` (59), `BioReference` (29). Three surfaces were worse for it — the Timeline titled a lab draw **"Quest Diagnostics results"**, the Biomarkers browser's panel facet filtered by lab **vendor**, and a single-analyte detail page was a dead end — and all three wanted the same missing thing: a `canonical_name → panel` resolver. This mints it once, as infrastructure, and wires the three low-risk consumers. #1499's Results-hub grouping keys on the same resolved `PanelId` later; none of its UI is built here.

## The taxonomy

`lib/biomarker-panels.ts` — pure, auth-blind, no DB.

- **Slug ids, not display strings.** A closed `PanelId` set with one `PANEL_LABELS: Record<PanelId, { label, order }>` owning the display string and sort order. The `?panel=` param stays a stable slug across rewording, a typo can't silently fork a group (unknown slug = type error), and reorder/reword is one edit — the `RULE_FINDING_PREFIXES` / `AppRoute` registry pattern.
- **34 clinical panels + the reserved `other`.** The issue quoted "28 panels", carried from #1499's draft — but #1499 cites #1502 for the table, so that number was never anchored to an actual assignment. The curated pass landed at **34**, the extra granularity going to orders that are genuinely drawn apart and would give a wrong impression if merged: `heavy-metals` vs `minerals` (a lead level must not sit beside a zinc level), `lipoprotein-particles` vs `lipids` (the NMR subfraction report is its own requisition), `hemoglobin-variants` vs `cbc`, `immunity-titers` vs `infectious-disease`. Where merging *was* honest it was taken — reproductive + adrenal/pituitary are one `hormones` panel, not two thin ones.
- **Assignment methodology.** Curated from routine ordering practice (which analytes arrive on one requisition / one report section), with every judgement call written down inline: the gestational glucose challenge sits in `glycemic` (it is a glucose measurement) while the NIPT set stays `prenatal-screening`; homocysteine sits in `inflammation` with hs-CRP/ESR, the CV-risk set it is ordered with, not in `vitamins` beside its B-vitamin cofactors; the hepatitis surface antibody stays with the hepatitis serology rather than the MMR/varicella `immunity-titers`; rheumatoid factor joins the immunoglobulins (it *is* an immunoglobulin assay) rather than minting a one-member autoimmune panel.
- **0 unmapped, and an exact bijection.** All **277** canonical names map; all 277 assignment members are real canonical names; none is assigned twice. `assigned.size === canonical.length` is asserted, so the three guards together pin a bijection.
- **Fallback posture.** `other` means "the taxonomy does not know this name" — an un-canonicalized analyte the extractor coined. It is explicitly **not** a bucket canonical entries may fall into: a pure test fails when any `canonical-biomarkers.json` entry resolves to `other`, so **a new canonical biomarker added without a panel breaks the build** instead of silently looking classified.
- **#482 interplay.** Panels answer a different question than `biomarkerFamily()` ("same order?" vs "same analyte?"), so they compose rather than compete: resolution is family-aware, and every spelling the family collapses shares one panel — `"Estimated Average Glucose"`/`"eAG"` resolve to `glycemic` exactly like `"Hemoglobin A1c"`, `"25-OH Vitamin D"` to `vitamins` exactly like `"Vitamin D, 25-Hydroxy"`. Two tests pin it: no registered family straddles two panels, and no two canonical entries the family collapses are assigned apart. Spot-checked both family tables; the D2/D3 fractions (deliberately *outside* the 25-OH family since #1193) are assigned explicitly and agree.
- **SQL realization (#394).** `panelKeyOfExpr()` inlines each panel's member spellings as an `IN (...)` preimage over the name expression — the same shape `biomarkerFamilyKey()` uses, generated from the same data, escaped literals only. Chosen over resolve-in-JS because the Timeline's grouping is a `GROUP BY` with aggregates and the facet is a `WHERE`; both need the answer inside SQL, and this is the existing code shape for exactly that. A test asserts the preimage and the JS matcher agree on every canonical name **and** every family spelling, so the two can never drift.

Data lands via the **generator**, not a hand-edit: the curated assignment is folded in by `curateBiomarkers()` (beside `RETEST_DAYS`/`AGE_BANDS`/`VELOCITY_PER_YEAR`) and `lib/canonical-biomarkers.json` was regenerated with `--curated-only`. The committed JSON stays a fixed point of that transform, and a test asserts its `panel` field agrees with the resolver row-for-row.

## Consumers, before → after

**1. Timeline event titles (`lib/timeline.ts`) — the visible one.**

| before | after |
|---|---|

## Summary

Follow-up to #563. You asked me to fix the Docker issue so the new Playwright specs (accessibility, passkey) could actually run instead of just typechecking. Did that — started Docker Desktop, a local Postgres container, and a `wrangler dev` (real Workerd runtime) instance, with your explicit consent for Prisma's `db push` safety gate. Running the tests for real surfaced genuine bugs, all fixed here.

### Real bugs found and fixed
- **`src/components/AuthPasskeyManager.tsx`** — `registerPasskey()` never checked the `/api/auth/passkey/register` GET response status before parsing it as WebAuthn options. Any error response (401, rate-limited, etc.) crashed with a bare `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'replace')` from inside `@simplewebauthn/browser` instead of a real error message — exactly what a user with an expired session would hit. Now checks `res.ok` first.
- **`scripts/reset-test-logins.mjs`** — `DELETE FROM "MfaChallenge"` referenced a table dropped from the schema in a prior cleanup commit but never updated here. This script was **completely broken** (verified: throws `relation "MfaChallenge" does not exist` on a fresh DB). Removed the dead statement; verified it now seeds all 5 test accounts cleanly.
- **`e2e/auth.spec.ts`** — three assertions referenced `/home` as the post-login page and a `.wb-root` selector, both retired when the Workbench system was replaced by Listen/Events/Pages (`WORKBENCH_PATH = '/listen'`). Verified directly against real `wrangler dev` that `/listen` — not `/home` — is the actual gated/authenticated destination. Updated all three assertions.

### Verified working (not a bug)
Registered a passkey and signed in with it end-to-end — real browser, Chromium's CDP WebAuthn virtual authenticator, real Postgres, real Workerd runtime. The application flow genuinely works; every earlier failure was my own local test-harness setup (mismatched secrets, wrong base URL baked into the build, local rate-limiter emulation issues), not app bugs.

### Documented, not fixed — needs your call
CI's gated "Extended authenticated E2E suite" runs against plain `npm run dev`, but `src/lib/db.ts` intentionally imports the wasm/workerd-only Prisma engine (to avoid a documented prior production outage). That engine can't load under plain `next dev`, so **any** authenticated request — not just passkey ones — 401s there, because `auth()`'s `jwt` callback does a DB read on every request. This means `auth.spec.ts`'s pre-existing OTP-login test, its `TEST_SESSION_COOKIE` test, and the new `passkey.spec.ts` all cannot currently pass in CI even once `E2E_ENABLED` and secrets are supplied. Documented prominently in both spec files. The real fix — pointing CI's authenticated E2E stage at `wrangler dev`/workerd instead of `next dev` — is a bigger infra decision than I should make unilaterally in this PR.

Also noted but deliberately not changed: `src/app/home/page.tsx`'s `redirect('/listen')` didn't reliably update the browser address bar in manual testing (page content did change) across both `next dev` and real Workerd — reproducible, but I don't have a confident root cause, so `e2e/auth.spec.ts` now tests `/listen` directly instead of routing through this ambiguous legacy alias.

body:
Backend half of populating UI form options from the database. Paired with eccn-management-ui-service-angular#17, which consumes this endpoint.

## Why this was needed

`product.service.ts` in the Angular app already called `GET /api/products/categories`. **That endpoint did not exist**, so the call 404'd. Digging further, the `Product` model had no category concept at all:

```java
private String name, description, status;
private List<String> features;
private List<VersionRelease> versions;
```

Which is why the frontend synthesises one — `row.category || features[0] || 'Software'` — and why product lists could show a *feature* in the CATEGORY column.

## Changes

- **`Product.category`**, nullable. Documents written before this field read back `null`; MongoDB is schemaless so no migration is needed.
- **`ProductService.getDistinctCategories()`** — distinct, non-blank, trimmed, sorted. Derived from stored products rather than a fixed enum, so the UI only ever offers categories that products actually use.
- **`GET /api/products/categories`**.

It returns `[]` today, because nothing is categorised yet. That is deliberate, not a defect: the client falls back to its own options rather than rendering an empty select, and the list becomes real as products are created with categories.

## Risk

GitNexus impact on `Product` before the change: **MEDIUM** — 14 impacted symbols, 8 direct, 2 execution flows (`updateProduct`, `markVersionAsClassified`). The field is purely additive, so existing dependents are unaffected. Confirmed by the full suite: **91 tests, 0 failures** (88 before, +3 new).

## Test-first

The test was written before the implementation and failed on `cannot find symbol: setCategory`. Beyond the happy path it pins two things worth keeping:

- **`/categories` is not shadowed by `/{id}`** on the same controller — otherwise the lookup would be handled as a product whose id is "categories" and return 404.
- **duplicates collapse, and `null`/blank categories are excluded**, so the dropdown never offers a value no product uses.

body:
## The failure

A subscription with this filter policy receives **nothing** — not "the wrong messages", nothing at all:

```json
{"store": [{"exists": false}]}
```

```
attribute absent   ->  not delivered   (AWS delivers)
attribute present  ->  not delivered   (correct)
```

Both branches decline, so the subscriber is permanently dead.

## Root cause

`ministack/services/sns.py:1477-1479` returned `False` the moment a policy key was missing from the published message attributes, before any rule for that key was looked at:

```python
attr = message_attributes.get(key)
if attr is None:
    return False
```

`exists: false` is evaluated against **presence**, not against a value, so it can never be reached from that branch. The `exists: true` half was already implemented in `_attr_matches_any`, which is why the gap is easy to miss.

## Why this is a bug rather than an intentional gap

MiniStack's own EventBridge matcher implements the same operator correctly, with a comment that describes exactly what SNS gets wrong — `ministack/services/eventbridge.py:1058-1073`:

> `[{"exists": true|false}]` is evaluated against key presence/absence, NOT against the value, so an absent key must NOT short-circuit to False before that check.

Same project, same operator, one surface has it and the other doesn't.

No open issue or PR mentions SNS filter policies.

## The fix

Nine lines in `_matches_filter_policy`: normalize the rule list first, then on an absent attribute check for an `{"exists": false}` rule and `continue` instead of returning. Present-attribute behaviour is untouched.

## How to test

```
hypercorn ministack.app:app --bind 127.0.0.1:4566 &
pytest tests/test_sns.py -q          # 85 passed
```

One test added — `test_sns_filter_policy_exists_false_matches_absent_attribute` — using boto3 with an SQS subscriber, in the style of the neighbouring `test_sns_filter_policy_blocks_non_matching`. It asserts both directions: attribute present ⇒ not delivered, attribute absent ⇒ delivered.

Regression proof — source reverted, server restarted on clean source, test kept:

```
>       assert len(msgs2.get("Messages", [])) == 1, "Message without the attribute must be delivered"
E       AssertionError: Message without the attribute must be delivered
E       assert 0 == 1
FAILED tests/test_sns.py::test_sns_filter_policy_exists_false_matches_absent_attribute
```

CHANGELOG `Unreleased → Fixed` entry included per the PR checklist.

## What I could not verify

**My baseline is not green.** This machine has no Docker, so 96 tests that need a Lambda/ECS/MWAA container fail before any change of mine. The SNS surface itself is 100% green, and `_matches_filter_policy` is reachable only from `_fanout`, but I want to state plainly that "no regressions" here rests on before/after diffing rather than on a fully green run.

Full-suite diff after the fix: my test flipped fail→pass, `test_cfn_apigwv2_full_http_api_stack_invokes_lambda` also flipped to pass, and 5 apigateway/appsync tests flipped to fail. Re-running those 5 in isolation **on the clean stashed tree** also fails 3 of them, with a different split per invocation — they are order/state-dependent flakes inside the already-broken Docker-dependent cluster, and none of them touch SNS.

**No AWS ground truth.** I have no credentials to check `exists: false` against real SNS. The justification is AWS's published filter-policy semantics plus MiniStack's own EventBridge implementation. If SNS deliberately diverges here, this PR is wrong — but nothing in the code or docs says so.

## Adjacent bugs I did not touch

Same function, all real, all separate changes — happy to file issues if useful:

- `FilterPolicyScope: MessageBody` returns `True` unconditionally; message-body filtering is not implemented at all
- `anything-but` compares strings against numeric list members
- `_check_numeric` silently ignores a trailing lone operator

author: thesaiearanti
body:
### Summary

`function_schema` compares parameter defaults (and annotations) to `inspect._empty` with `==`/`!=`, which invokes the user-supplied value's `__eq__`. Two observable failures on valid Python functions:

1. **Crash at decoration time** — a default with elementwise equality semantics (a numpy array is the canonical case) makes `default != inspect._empty` return an array, whose truthiness raises:
   ```python
   @function_tool
   def score(x: int, weights: Any = np.array([1.0, 2.0])) -> int: ...
   # ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous.
   ```
   Verified with real numpy; the regression test uses a dependency-free stub with the same `__eq__` shape.

2. **Silent contract violation** — a default whose `__eq__` answers `True` (mocks, sentinels, some DSL objects) satisfies `default == inspect._empty`, so the parameter is marked **required** in the schema and its default silently discarded.

The `inspect` module's documented convention is identity comparison (`param.default is Parameter.empty`); the sentinel is a unique object precisely so user values can never influence the check. This PR switches all five sentinel comparisons in the file to `is`/`is not` — the two default checks above (the observable bugs) and the three annotation checks, which carry the same latent hazard. Identity is behavior-preserving for every value without a pathological `__eq__`.

### Test plan

- Two regression tests with pure-Python stubs (no numpy dependency): an elementwise-`__eq__` default must build a schema, stay optional, and round-trip through `to_call_args`; an always-`True`-`__eq__` default must not be marked required. Both fail on `main` and pass with the fix.
- `make format`, `make lint`, `make typecheck`, `make tests` all pass.

### Issue number

None — found by reading `function_schema.py` (same pass that produced #3956).

body:
## Summary

This is the first branch in which the **colorization half of the product executed against real data at all**. Ten phases had produced an excellent MangaDex reader, but PRD §1 step 2 — applying Visual DNA — had never once run. It runs now, end to end, and the first contact with real footage immediately found a serious bug.

Pilot input: 3 Chainsaw Man episodes supplied locally by the repo owner.

## The bug this exists to justify

`ColorPaletteClustering` used `MiniBatchKMeans.partial_fit` per batch. That estimator's per-center learning rate decays as roughly 1/(samples seen), and `DNAExtractor` hands it ~8.4M pixels in the very first call — so after batch 1, every later batch moved the centroids by a negligible amount. **The palette was decided by the first batch and essentially nothing else.**

In file order, batch 1 is episode 1 frames 0–31: production logos and a black cold open. The result was eight near-black centroids, several collapsed onto identical points, and `validate_centroids` passed all of it.

The tell-tale symptom was that **more data made it worse** — 1,499 frames produced a better palette than 4,590. Measured directly: over 20 sequential batches, centroid brightness stayed frozen at 81.5 → 83.9 while incoming batch brightness swung between 41 and 100.

**Fix:** reservoir-sample into a bounded pool, then a single full `KMeans.fit` — order-independent by construction. Verified by reproducing an independently computed plain `sklearn.KMeans` palette on the same pixels: same colours, different ordering.

It survived 285 passing tests and a schema validator. Only real footage caught it. Had it gone unnoticed, a black palette would have fed into LoRA training and colorization, producing a bad result with no way to tell whether the premise or the plumbing was at fault.

## What's closed

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| 11.2 lawful frame source | Video files the owner holds; `LocalFileStrategy` already covered it, no new code |
| 11.3 retire pirated-stream path | −1,029 lines (`consumet_client`, `hls_stream_handler`, `APIStreamStrategy`, settings, `.env`, tests). `VideoSourceStrategy` ABC kept so a lawful remote source can be added later |
| 11.4 headless OpenCV | Reclaimed 4.13.0.92. The GUI build had won *and* drifted to 5.0 — every test was running on a major version it wasn't written for. `make fix-opencv` prevents regression |
| 11.5 pilot series | Chainsaw Man: 97/100 chapters readable on MangaDex. An Official Colored edition exists, giving the upcoming quality gate a publisher-authored reference instead of a purely subjective call |
| 12.1 extraction | 4,590 frames from 3 episodes in 6m28s, peak RSS ~400 MB |
| 12.2 manifest | 46 batch files, 2.3 GB, at the documented convention |
| 12.3 / 12.4 palette | Bug above. `k` raised 8 → 16 behind a new `dna_n_clusters` setting — at k=8, clusters are allocated by screen area, so neutral backgrounds crowded out every saturated identity colour (no blue and no blonde appeared at all) |
| 12.5 / 12.6 persistence | One real `anime_dna` row via the real Celery task — 1.2B pixel samples in ~70s, RSS flat at 981 MB, registered in `celery_jobs` per rule A12 |
| 13.3 ControlNet | `lllyasviel/sd-controlnet-lineart` **does not exist** (HF returns 401) and would have been 768-dim anyway. Now `xinsir/controlnet-scribble-sdxl-1.0` — 2048-dim, standard layout, loads through the existing pipeline factory unchanged |
